blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: 7.1 Introduction

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Differential Calculus is centred on the concept of the
derivative. The original motivation for the derivative was
the problem of defining tangent lines to the graphs of
functions and calculating the slope of such lines. Integral
Calculus is motivated by the problem of defining and
calculating the area of the region bounded by the graph of
the functions.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
If a function $f$ is differentiable in an interval I, i.e., its
derivative $f'$ exists at each point of I, then a natural question
arises that given $f'$ at each point of I, can we determine
the function? The functions that could possibly have given
function as a derivative are called anti derivatives (or
primitive) of the function. Further, the formula that gives
all these anti derivatives is called the *indefinite integral* of the function and such
process of finding anti derivatives is called integration. Such type of problems arise in
many practical situations. For instance, if we know the instantaneous velocity of an
object at any instant, then there arises a natural question, i.e., can we determine the
position of the object at any instant? There are several such practical and theoretical
situations where the process of integration is involved. The development of integral
calculus arises out of the efforts of solving the problems of the following types:

blocks.label: List
blocks.text:
(a) the problem of finding a function whenever its derivative is given,
(b) the problem of finding the area bounded by the graph of a function under certain
conditions.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
These two problems lead to the two forms of the integrals, e.g., indefinite and
definite integrals, which together constitute the \textbf{\textit{Integral Calculus}}.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
There is a connection, known as the *Fundamental Theorem of Calculus*, between
indefinite integral and definite integral which makes the definite integral as a practical
tool for science and engineering. The definite integral is also used to solve many interesting
problems from various disciplines like economics, finance and probability.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
In this Chapter, we shall confine ourselves to the study of indefinite and definite
integrals and their elementary properties including some techniques of integration.

blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: 7.2 Integration as an Inverse Process of Differentiation

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Integration is the inverse process of differentiation. Instead of differentiating a function,
we are given the derivative of a function and asked to find its primitive, i.e., the original
function. Such a process is called $integration$ or $anti$ $differentiation$.
Let us consider the following examples:

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: We know that $\frac{d}{dx}(\sin x) = \cos x$ ... (1)

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \frac{d}{dx} \left( \frac{x^3}{3} \right) = x^2 \quad \dots (2) $$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: and $\frac{d}{dx}(e^x) = e^x$ ... (3)

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
We observe that in (1), the function $\cos x$ is the derived function of $\sin x$. We say

that $\sin x$ is an anti derivative (or an integral) of $\cos x$. Similarly, in (2) and (3), $\frac{x^3}{3}$ and

$e^x$ are the anti derivatives (or integrals) of $x^2$ and $e^x$, respectively. Again, we note that

for any real number C, treated as constant function, its derivative is zero and hence, we

can write (1), (2) and (3) as follows :

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $\frac{d}{dx}(\sin x + C) = \cos x$, $\frac{d}{dx}(\frac{x^3}{3} + C) = x^2$ and $\frac{d}{dx}(e^x + C) = e^x$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Thus, anti derivatives (or integrals) of the above cited functions are not unique.
Actually, there exist infinitely many anti derivatives of each of these functions which
can be obtained by choosing C arbitrarily from the set of real numbers. For this reason
C is customarily referred to as \textbf{\textit{arbitrary constant}}. In fact, C is the \textbf{\textit{parameter}} by
varying which one gets different anti derivatives (or integrals) of the given function.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
More generally, if there is a function F such that $\frac{d}{dx} \mathrm{F} (x) = f (x) , \forall x \in \mathrm{I} (interval)$,
then for any arbitrary real number C, (also called constant of integration)

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \frac{d}{dx} [\mathrm{F}(x) + \mathrm{C}] = f(x), x \in \mathrm{I} $$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Thus, $\qquad \{F + C, C \in \mathbf{R}\}$ denotes a family of anti derivatives of $f$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
*Remark* Functions with same derivatives differ by a constant. To show this, let $g$ and $h$
be two functions having the same derivatives on an interval $I$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Consider the function $f = g - h$ defined by $f(x) = g(x) - h(x)$, $\forall x \in \mathrm{I}$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Then $\frac{df}{dx} = f' = g' - h'$ giving $f'(x) = g'(x) - h'(x) \forall x \in \mathrm{I}$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: or $f'(x) = 0, \forall x \in \mathrm{I}$ by hypothesis,

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: i.e., the rate of change of $f$ with respect to $x$ is zero on I and hence $f$ is constant.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
In view of the above remark, it is justified to infer that the family $\{ \mathrm{F} + \mathrm{C}, \mathrm{C} \in \mathbf{R} \}$
provides all possible anti derivatives of $f$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
We introduce a new symbol, namely, $\int f(x) dx$ which will represent the entire
class of anti derivatives read as the indefinite integral of $f$ with respect to $x$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Symbolically, we write $\int f(x) dx = \mathrm{F}(x) + \mathrm{C}.$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: **Notation** Given that $\frac{dy}{dx} = f(x)$, we write $y = \int f(x) dx$.

blocks.text:

blocks.label: Sub-section-title
blocks.text: 7.2.1 Some properties of indefinite integral

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: In this sub section, we shall derive some properties of indefinite integrals.

blocks.label: List
blocks.text:
(I) The process of differentiation and integration are inverses of each other in the
sense of the following results :

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \frac{d}{dx} \int f(x) dx = f(x) $$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: and $\int f'(x) \, dx = f(x) + C$, where $C$ is any arbitrary constant.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Proof Let F be any anti derivative of $f$, i.e.,

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \frac{d}{dx} \mathbf{F}(x) = f(x) $$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Then $\int f(x) dx = F(x) + C$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Therefore $\frac{d}{dx} \int f(x) dx = \frac{d}{dx} (\mathrm{F}(x) + \mathrm{C})$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ = \frac{d}{dx} \mathrm{F} (x) = f (x) $$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Similarly, we note that

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$f'(x) = \frac{d}{dx} f(x)$$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: and hence $\int f'(x) dx = f(x) + C$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: where C is arbitrary constant called constant of integration.

blocks.label: List
blocks.text:
(II) Two indefinite integrals with the same derivative lead to the same family of
curves and so they are equivalent.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Proof Let $f$ and $g$ be two functions such that

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \frac{d}{dx} \int f(x) dx = \frac{d}{dx} \int g(x) dx $$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: or $\frac{d}{dx}\left[\int f(x) dx-\int g(x) dx\right]=0$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Hence $\int f(x) dx - \int g(x) dx = \text{C}$, where C is any real number (Why?)

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: or $\int f(x) dx = \int g(x) dx + C$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: So the families of curves $\left\{\int f(x) \, dx + \mathrm{C}_1, \mathrm{C}_1 \in \mathrm{R}\right\}$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: and $\quad\left\{\int g(x) \, dx + \mathrm{C}_2, \mathrm{C}_2 \in \mathrm{R}\right\}$ are identical.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Hence, in this sense, $\int f(x) dx$ and $\int g(x) dx$ are equivalent.

blocks.label: Infobox
blocks.text:
Note The equivalence of the families $\left\{\int f(x) dx + C_1, C_1 \in \mathbf{R}\right\}$ and
$\left\{\int g(x) dx + C_2, C_2 \in \mathbf{R}\right\}$ is customarily expressed by writing $\int f(x) dx = \int g(x) dx$,
without mentioning the parameter.

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: (III) $\int [f(x) + g(x)] dx = \int f(x) dx + \int g(x) dx$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Proof By Property (I), we have

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \frac{d}{dx} \left[ \int [f(x) + g(x)] dx \right] = f(x) + g(x) \qquad \dots (1) $$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: On the otherhand, we find that

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
$$ \frac{d}{dx} \left[ \int f(x) \, dx + \int g(x) \, dx \right] = \frac{d}{dx} \int f(x) \, dx + \frac{d}{dx} \int g(x) \, dx $$
$$ = f(x) + g(x) \qquad \dots (2) $$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Thus, in view of Property (II), it follows by (1) and (2) that

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \int ( f(x) + g(x) ) dx = \int f(x) dx + \int g(x) dx . $$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: (IV) For any real number $k$, $\int k f(x) dx = k \int f(x) dx$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Proof By the Property (I), $\frac{d}{dx} \int k f(x) dx = k f(x)$.

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Also $$\frac{d}{dx}\left[k \int f(x) \, dx\right] = k \frac{d}{dx} \int f(x) \, dx = k f(x)$$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Therefore, using the Property (II), we have $\int k f(x) dx = k \int f(x) dx$.

blocks.label: List
blocks.text:
(V) Properties (III) and (IV) can be generalised to a finite number of functions
$f_1, f_2, ..., f_n$ and the real numbers, $k_1, k_2, ..., k_n$ giving

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \int \left[ k_1 f_1(x) + k_2 f_2(x) + \dots + k_n f_n(x) \right] dx $$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ = k_1 \int f_1(x) \, dx + k_2 \int f_2(x) \, dx + \dots + k_n \int f_n(x) \, dx . $$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
To find an anti derivative of a given function, we search intuitively for a function
whose derivative is the given function. The search for the requisite function for finding
an anti derivative is known as integration by the method of inspection. We illustrate it
through some examples.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 1 Write an anti derivative for each of the following functions using the
method of inspection:

blocks.label: List
blocks.text: (i) $\cos 2x$ (ii) $3x^2 + 4x^3$ (iii) $\frac{1}{x}, x \neq 0$

blocks.label: Sub-section-title
blocks.text: Solution

blocks.label: List
blocks.text: (i) We look for a function whose derivative is $\cos 2x$. Recall that

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \frac{d}{dx} \sin 2x = 2 \cos 2x $$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: or $\cos 2x = \frac{1}{2} \frac{d}{dx} (\sin 2x) = \frac{d}{dx} \left( \frac{1}{2} \sin 2x \right)$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Therefore, an anti derivative of $\cos 2x$ is $\frac{1}{2} \sin 2x$.

blocks.label: List
blocks.text: (ii) We look for a function whose derivative is $3x^2 + 4x^3$. Note that

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \frac{d}{dx} \left( x^3 + x^4 \right) = 3x^2 + 4x^3. $$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Therefore, an anti derivative of $3x^2 + 4x^3$ is $x^3 + x^4$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: (iii) We know that

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \frac{d}{dx} (\log x) = \frac{1}{x}, x > 0 \text{ and } \frac{d}{dx} [\log (-x)] = \frac{1}{-x} (-1) = \frac{1}{x}, x < 0 $$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Combining above, we get $\frac{d}{dx}(\log|x|)=\frac{1}{x}, x \neq 0$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Therefore, $\int_{\frac{1}{x}}^{\frac{1}{x}} dx = \log |x|$ is one of the anti derivatives of $\frac{1}{x}$.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 2 Find the following integrals:

(i) $\int \frac{x^3 - 1}{x^2} dx$      (ii) $\int (x^{\frac{2}{3}} + 1) dx$      (iii) $\int (x^{\frac{3}{2}} + 2 e^x - \frac{1}{x}) dx$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Solution

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: (i) We have

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
$\int \frac{x^{3}-1}{x^{2}} d x=\int x d x-\int x^{-2} d x$ (by Property V)

$=\left(\frac{x^{1+1}}{1+1}+\mathrm{C}_{1}\right)-\left(\frac{x^{-2+1}}{-2+1}+\mathrm{C}_{2}\right) ; \mathrm{C}_{1}, \mathrm{C}_{2}$ are constants of integration

$=\frac{x^{2}}{2}+\mathrm{C}_{1}-\frac{x^{-1}}{-1}-\mathrm{C}_{2}=\frac{x^{2}}{2}+\frac{1}{x}+\mathrm{C}_{1}-\mathrm{C}_{2}$

$=\frac{x^{2}}{2}+\frac{1}{x}+\mathrm{C}$, where $\mathrm{C}=\mathrm{C}_{1}-\mathrm{C}_{2}$ is another constant of integration.

blocks.label: Infobox
blocks.text:
Note From now onwards, we shall write only one constant of integration in the
final answer.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: (ii) We have

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
(iii) We have $\int (x^2 + 2 e^x - \frac{1}{x}) dx = \int x^{\frac{3}{2}} dx + \int 2 e^x dx - \int \frac{1}{x} dx$


$$= \frac{x^{\frac{3}{2}+1}}{\frac{3}{2}+1} + 2 e^x - \log |x| + C$$


$$= \frac{2}{5} x^{\frac{5}{2}} + 2 e^x - \log |x| + C$$

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 3 Find the following integrals:

(i) $\int (\sin x + \cos x) dx$      (ii) $\int \text{cosec } x (\text{cosec } x + \cot x) dx$

(iii) $\int \frac{1 - \sin x}{\cos^2 x} dx$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Solution

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
(i) We have
$$\int (\sin x + \cos x) dx = \int \sin x dx + \int \cos x dx$$
$$= -\cos x + \sin x + C$$

blocks.label: List
blocks.text:
(ii) We have
$$\int (\operatorname{cosec} x (\operatorname{cosec} x + \cot x) \, dx = \int \operatorname{cosec}^2 x \, dx + \int \operatorname{cosec} x \cot x \, dx$$
$$= -\cot x - \operatorname{cosec} x + C$$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
(iii) We have

$$ \int \frac{1 - \sin x}{\cos^2 x} dx = \int \frac{1}{\cos^2 x} dx - \int \frac{\sin x}{\cos^2 x} dx $$

$$ = \int \sec^2 x dx - \int \tan x \sec x dx $$

$$ = \tan x - \sec x + C $$

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 4 Find the anti derivative F of $f$ defined by $f(x) = 4x^3 - 6$, where F (0) = 3

Solution One anti derivative of $f(x)$ is $x^4 - 6x$ since

$$\frac{d}{dx}(x^4 - 6x) = 4x^3 - 6$$

Therefore, the anti derivative F is given by

$$\text{F}(x) = x^4 - 6x + \text{C}, \text{ where C is constant.}$$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Given that $F(0) = 3$, which gives,

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$3 = 0 - 6 \times 0 + C \quad \text{or} \quad C = 3$$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Hence, the required anti derivative is the unique function $F$ defined by

blocks.label: Sub-section-title
blocks.text: Remarks

blocks.label: List
blocks.text:
(i) We see that if F is an anti derivative of $f$, then so is F + C, where C is any
constant. Thus, if we know one anti derivative F of a function $f$, we can write
down an infinite number of anti derivatives of $f$ by adding any constant to F
expressed by F($x$) + C, C $\in$ $\mathbf{R}$. In applications, it is often necessary to satisfy an
additional condition which then determines a specific value of C giving unique
anti derivative of the given function.
(ii) Sometimes, F is not expressible in terms of elementary functions viz., polynomial,
logarithmic, exponential, trigonometric functions and their inverses etc. We are
therefore blocked for finding $\int f(x) dx$. For example, it is not possible to find
$\int e^{-x^2} dx$ by inspection since we can not find a function whose derivative is $e^{-x^2}$
(iii) When the variable of integration is denoted by a variable other than $x$, the integral
formulae are modified accordingly. For instance
$$\int y^4 dy = \frac{y^{4+1}}{4+1} + \text{C} = \frac{1}{5} y^5 + \text{C}$$

blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: 7.3 Methods of Integration

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
In previous section, we discussed integrals of those functions which were readily
obtainable from derivatives of some functions. It was based on inspection, i.e., on the
search of a function $F$ whose derivative is $f$ which led us to the integral of $f$. However,
this method, which depends on inspection, is not very suitable for many functions.
Hence, we need to develop additional techniques or methods for finding the integrals
by reducing them into standard forms. Prominent among them are methods based on:

blocks.label: List
blocks.text:
1. Integration by Substitution
2. Integration using Partial Fractions
3. Integration by Parts

blocks.label: Sub-section-title
blocks.text: 7.3.1 Integration by substitution

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: In this section, we consider the method of integration by substitution.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
The given integral $\int f(x) dx$ can be transformed into another form by changing
the independent variable $x$ to $t$ by substituting $x = g(t)$.

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Consider $I = \int f(x) dx$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Put $x = g(t)$ so that $\frac{dx}{dt} = g'(t)$.

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: We write $dx = g'(t) dt$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Thus $I = \int f(x) dx = \int f(g(t)) g'(t) dt$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
This change of variable formula is one of the important tools available to us in the
name of integration by substitution. It is often important to guess what will be the useful
substitution. Usually, we make a substitution for a function whose derivative also occurs
in the integrand as illustrated in the following examples.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 5 Integrate the following functions w.r.t. $x$:

(i) $\sin mx$                                     (ii) $2x \sin (x^2 + 1)$

(iii) $\frac{\tan^4 \sqrt{x} \sec^2 \sqrt{x}}{\sqrt{x}}$           (iv) $\frac{\sin (\tan^{-1} x)}{1 + x^2}$

blocks.label: Sub-section-title
blocks.text: Solution

blocks.label: List
blocks.text:
(i) We know that derivative of $mx$ is $m$. Thus, we make the substitution
$mx = t$ so that $mdx = dt$.

Therefore, $\int \sin mx \, dx = \frac{1}{m} \int \sin t \, dt = -\frac{1}{m} \cos t + \text{C} = -\frac{1}{m} \cos mx + \text{C}$

(ii) Derivative of $x^2 + 1$ is $2x$. Thus, we use the substitution $x^2 + 1 = t$ so that
$2x \, dx = dt$.

Therefore, $\int 2x \sin (x^2 + 1) \, dx = \int \sin t \, dt = -\cos t + \text{C} = -\cos (x^2 + 1) + \text{C}$

(iii) Derivative of $\sqrt{x}$ is $\frac{1}{2} x^{-\frac{1}{2}} = \frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}}$. Thus, we use the substitution

$\sqrt{x} = t$ so that $\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}} \, dx = dt$ giving $dx = 2t \, dt$.

Thus, $\int \frac{\tan^4 \sqrt{x} \sec^2 \sqrt{x}}{\sqrt{x}} \, dx = \int \frac{2t \tan^4 t \sec^2 t \, dt}{t} = 2 \int \tan^4 t \sec^2 t \, dt$

Again, we make another substitution $\tan t = u$ so that $\sec^2 t \, dt = du$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
Therefore, $2 \int \tan^4 t \sec^2 t \, dt = 2 \int u^4 \, du = 2 \frac{u^5}{5} + \text{C}$
$= \frac{2}{5} \tan^5 t + \text{C}$ (since $u = \tan t$)
$= \frac{2}{5} \tan^5 \sqrt{x} + \text{C}$ (since $t = \sqrt{x}$)

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Hence, $\int \frac{\tan ^4 \sqrt{x} \sec ^2 \sqrt{x}}{\sqrt{x}} d x=\frac{2}{5} \tan ^5 \sqrt{x}+\mathrm{C}$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Alternatively, make the substitution $\tan \sqrt{x} = t$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: (iv) Derivative of $\tan^{-1}x = \frac{1}{1+x^2}$. Thus, we use the substitution

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$\tan^{-1} x = t \text{ so that } \frac{dx}{1 + x^2} = dt.$$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Therefore , $\int \frac{\sin (\tan^{-1} x)}{1+x^{2}} d x=\int \sin t d t=-\cos t+\mathrm{C}=-\cos (\tan ^{-1} x)+\mathrm{C}$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Now, we discuss some important integrals involving trigonometric functions and
their standard integrals using substitution technique. These will be used later without
reference.

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: (i) $\int \tan x \, dx = \log |\sec x| + \mathrm{C}$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: We have

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \int \tan x \, dx = \int \frac{\sin x}{\cos x} \, dx $$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Put $\cos x = t$ so that $\sin x \, dx = - \, dt$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Then $$\int \tan x \, dx = -\int \frac{dt}{t} = -\log |t| + C = -\log |\cos x| + C$$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: or $$\int \tan x \, dx = \log |\sec x| + \mathrm{C}$$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: (ii) $\int \cot x \, dx = \log |\sin x| + \mathrm{C}$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: We have $\int \cot x \, dx = \int \frac{\cos x}{\sin x} \, dx$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Put $\sin x = t$ so that $\cos x \, dx = dt$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Then $\int \cot x \, dx = \int \frac{dt}{t} = \log |t| + C = \log |\sin x| + C$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: (iii) $\int \sec x \, dx = \log |\sec x + \tan x| + \mathrm{C}$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: We have

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \int \sec x \, dx = \int \frac{\sec x (\sec x + \tan x)}{\sec x + \tan x} \, dx $$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Put $\sec x + \tan x = t$ so that $\sec x (\tan x + \sec x) dx = dt$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Therefore, $\int \sec x \, dx = \int \frac{dt}{t} = \log |t| + \mathrm{C} = \log |\sec x + \tan x| + \mathrm{C}$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: (iv) $\int \operatorname{cosec} x \, dx = \log |\operatorname{cosec} x - \cot x| + \mathrm{C}$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: We have

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \int \operatorname{cosec} x \ dx = \int \frac{\operatorname{cosec} x (\operatorname{cosec} x + \cot x)}{(\operatorname{cosec} x + \cot x)} \ dx $$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Put $\operatorname{cosec} x + \cot x = t$ so that $-\operatorname{cosec} x (\operatorname{cosec} x + \cot x) dx = dt$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
So $\int \operatorname{cosec} x \, dx = -\int \frac{dt}{t} = -\log |t| = -\log |\operatorname{cosec} x + \cot x| + \mathrm{C}$

$= -\log \left| \frac{\operatorname{cosec}^2 x - \cot^2 x}{\operatorname{cosec} x - \cot x} \right| + \mathrm{C}$

$= \log |\operatorname{cosec} x - \cot x| + \mathrm{C}$

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 6 Find the following integrals:

(i) $\int \sin^3 x \cos^2 x \, dx$ (ii) $\int \frac{\sin x}{\sin (x + a)} \, dx$ (iii) $\int \frac{1}{1 + \tan x} \, dx$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Solution

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: (i) We have

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
$$ \int \sin^3 x \cos^2 x \, dx = \int \sin^2 x \cos^2 x \, (\sin x) \, dx $$
$$ = \int (1 - \cos^2 x) \cos^2 x \, (\sin x) \, dx $$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Put $t = \cos x$ so that $dt = - \sin x \, dx$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
Therefore, $\int \sin^2 x \cos^2 x (\sin x) \, dx = -\int (1-t^2) t^2 \, dt$
$= -\int (t^2 - t^4) \, dt = -\left( \frac{t^3}{3} - \frac{t^5}{5} \right) + \text{C}$
$= -\frac{1}{3} \cos^3 x + \frac{1}{5} \cos^5 x + \text{C}$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: (ii) Put $x + a = t$. Then $dx = dt$. Therefore

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
$$ \int \frac{\sin x}{\sin (x+a)} dx = \int \frac{\sin (t-a)}{\sin t} dt $$

$$ = \int \frac{\sin t \cos a - \cos t \sin a}{\sin t} dt $$

$$ = \cos a \int dt - \sin a \int \cot t dt $$

$$ = (\cos a) t - (\sin a) \left[ \log |\sin t| + \text{C}_1 \right] $$

$$ = (\cos a) (x+a) - (\sin a) \left[ \log |\sin (x+a)| + \text{C}_1 \right] $$

$$ = x \cos a + a \cos a - (\sin a) \log |\sin (x+a)| - \text{C}_1 \sin a $$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Hence, $\int \frac{\sin x}{\sin (x+a)} dx = x \cos a - \sin a \log |\sin (x+a)| + C,$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: where, $C = - C_1 \sin a + a \cos a$, is another arbitrary constant.

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
(iii) $\int \frac{dx}{1 + \tan x} = \int \frac{\cos x \, dx}{\cos x + \sin x}$

$= \frac{1}{2} \int \frac{(\cos x + \sin x + \cos x - \sin x) \, dx}{\cos x + \sin x}$

$= \frac{1}{2} \int dx + \frac{1}{2} \int \frac{\cos x - \sin x}{\cos x + \sin x} \, dx$

$= \frac{x}{2} + \frac{C_1}{2} + \frac{1}{2} \int \frac{\cos x - \sin x}{\cos x + \sin x} \, dx$ ... (1)

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Now, consider $I = \int \frac{\cos x - \sin x}{\cos x + \sin x} dx$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Put $\cos x + \sin x = t$ so that $(\cos x - \sin x) dx = dt$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Therefore $I = \int \frac{dt}{t} = \log |t| + C_2 = \log |\cos x + \sin x| + C_2$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Putting it in (1), we get

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
$$ \int \frac{dx}{1 + \tan x} = \frac{x}{2} + \frac{\text{C}_1}{2} + \frac{1}{2} \log |\cos x + \sin x| + \frac{\text{C}_2}{2} $$

$$ = \frac{x}{2} + \frac{1}{2} \log |\cos x + \sin x| + \frac{\text{C}_1}{2} + \frac{\text{C}_2}{2} $$

$$ = \frac{x}{2} + \frac{1}{2} \log |\cos x + \sin x| + \text{C}, \left( \text{C} = \frac{\text{C}_1}{2} + \frac{\text{C}_2}{2} \right) $$

blocks.label: Sub-section-title
blocks.text: 7.3.2 Integration using trigonometric identities

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
When the integrand involves some trigonometric functions, we use some known identities
to find the integral as illustrated through the following example.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text: Example 7 Find (i) $\int \cos^2 x \, dx$   (ii) $\int \sin 2x \cos 3x \, dx$   (iii) $\int \sin^3 x \, dx$

blocks.label: Sub-section-title
blocks.text: Solution

blocks.label: List
blocks.text: (i) Recall the identity $\cos 2x = 2 \cos^2 x - 1$, which gives

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \cos^2 x = \frac{1 + \cos 2x}{2} $$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
Therefore, $\int \cos^2 x \, dx = \frac{1}{2} \int (1 + \cos 2x) \, dx = \frac{1}{2} \int dx + \frac{1}{2} \int \cos 2x \, dx$
$= \frac{x}{2} + \frac{1}{4} \sin 2x + \text{C}$

blocks.label: List
blocks.text: (ii) Recall the identity $\sin x \cos y = \frac{1}{2} [\sin (x + y) + \sin (x - y)]$ (Why?)

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
Then $\int \sin 2x \cos 3x dx = \frac{1}{2} \left[ \int \sin 5x dx - \int \sin x dx \right]$
$= \frac{1}{2} \left[ -\frac{1}{5} \cos 5x + \cos x \right] + C$
$= -\frac{1}{10} \cos 5x + \frac{1}{2} \cos x + C$

blocks.label: List
blocks.text: (iii) From the identity $\sin 3x = 3 \sin x - 4 \sin^3 x$, we find that

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$\sin^3 x = \frac{3\sin x - \sin 3x}{4}$$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
Therefore, $\int \sin^3 x \, dx = \frac{3}{4} \int \sin x \, dx - \frac{1}{4} \int \sin 3x \, dx$
$= -\frac{3}{4} \cos x + \frac{1}{12} \cos 3x + \text{C}$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Alternatively, $\int \sin^3 x \, dx = \int \sin^2 x \sin x \, dx = \int (1 - \cos^2 x) \sin x \, dx$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Put $\cos x = t$ so that $-\sin x dx = dt$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
Therefore, $\int \sin^3 x \, dx = -\int (1-t^2) \, dt = -\int dt + \int t^2 \, dt = -t + \frac{t^3}{3} + \text{C}$

$= -\cos x + \frac{1}{3} \cos^3 x + \text{C}$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: $Remark$ It can be shown using trigonometric identities that both answers are equivalent.

blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: 7.4 Integrals of Some Particular Functions

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
In this section, we mention below some important formulae of integrals and apply them
for integrating many other related standard integrals:

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: (1) $\int \frac{dx}{x^2 - a^2} = \frac{1}{2a} \log \left| \frac{x - a}{x + a} \right| + C$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: (2) $\int \frac{dx}{a^2 - x^2} = \frac{1}{2a} \log \left| \frac{a + x}{a - x} \right| + C$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: (3) $\int \frac{dx}{x^2 + a^2} = \frac{1}{a} \tan^{-1} \frac{x}{a} + \mathrm{C}$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: (4) $\int \frac{dx}{\sqrt{x^2 - a^2}} = \log \left| x + \sqrt{x^2 - a^2} \right| + C$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: (5) $\int \frac{dx}{\sqrt{a^2 - x^2}} = \sin^{-1} \frac{x}{a} + \mathrm{C}$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: (6) $\int \frac{dx}{\sqrt{x^2 + a^2}} = \log \left| x + \sqrt{x^2 + a^2} \right| + C$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: We now prove the above results:

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: (1) We have $\frac{1}{x^2-a^2}=\frac{1}{(x-a)(x+a)}$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$= \frac{1}{2a} \left[ \frac{(x+a) - (x-a)}{(x-a)(x+a)} \right] = \frac{1}{2a} \left[ \frac{1}{x-a} - \frac{1}{x+a} \right]$$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Therefore, $\int \frac{dx}{x^2 - a^2} = \frac{1}{2a} \left[ \int \frac{dx}{x - a} - \int \frac{dx}{x + a} \right]$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ = \frac{1}{2a} \log \left| \frac{x - a}{x + a} \right| + C $$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: (2) In view of (1) above, we have

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \frac{1}{a^2 - x^2} = \frac{1}{2a} \left[ \frac{(a+x) + (a-x)}{(a+x)(a-x)} \right] = \frac{1}{2a} \left[ \frac{1}{a-x} + \frac{1}{a+x} \right] $$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
Therefore, $\int \frac{dx}{a^2 - x^2} = \frac{1}{2a} \left[ \int \frac{dx}{a - x} + \int \frac{dx}{a + x} \right]$
$= \frac{1}{2a} [-\log |a - x| + \log |a + x|] + C$
$= \frac{1}{2a} \log \left| \frac{a + x}{a - x} \right| + C$

blocks.label: Infobox
blocks.text: Note The technique used in (1) will be explained in Section 7.5.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: (3) Put $x = a \tan \theta$. Then $dx = a \sec^2 \theta \, d\theta$.

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
Therefore, $\int \frac{dx}{x^2 + a^2} = \int \frac{a \sec^2 \theta \, d\theta}{a^2 \tan^2 \theta + a^2}$

$= \frac{1}{a} \int d\theta = \frac{1}{a} \theta + C = \frac{1}{a} \tan^{-1} \frac{x}{a} + C$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: (4) Let $x = a \sec\theta$. Then $dx = a \sec\theta \tan\theta d\theta$.

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
Therefore, $\int \frac{dx}{\sqrt{x^2-a^2}} = \int \frac{a \sec \theta \tan \theta \, d\theta}{\sqrt{a^2 \sec^2 \theta - a^2}}$

$= \int \sec \theta \, d\theta = \log |\sec \theta + \tan \theta| + \text{C}_1$

$= \log \left| \frac{x}{a} + \sqrt{\frac{x^2}{a^2} - 1} \right| + \text{C}_1$

$= \log \left| x + \sqrt{x^2 - a^2} \right| - \log |a| + \text{C}_1$

$= \log \left| x + \sqrt{x^2 - a^2} \right| + \text{C}_1$, where $\text{C} = \text{C}_1 - \log |a|$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: (5) Let $x = a \sin\theta$. Then $dx = a \cos\theta \mathrm{d}\theta$.

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
Therefore, $\int \frac{dx}{\sqrt{a^2 - x^2}} = \int \frac{a \cos \theta \, d\theta}{\sqrt{a^2 - a^2 \sin^2 \theta}}$
$= \int d\theta = \theta + C = \sin^{-1} \frac{x}{a} + C$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: (6) Let $x = a \tan \theta$. Then $dx = a \sec^2 \theta \mathrm{d} \theta$.

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
Therefore, $\int \frac{dx}{\sqrt{x^2 + a^2}} = \int \frac{a \sec^2 \theta \, d\theta}{\sqrt{a^2 \tan^2 \theta + a^2}}$
$= \int \sec \theta \, d\theta = \log |(\sec \theta + \tan \theta)| + C_1$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ = \log \left| \frac{x}{a} + \sqrt{\frac{x^2}{a^2} + 1} \right| + C_1 $$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ = \log \left| x + \sqrt{x^2 + a^2} \right| - \log | a | + C_1 $$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$= \log \left| x + \sqrt{x^2 + a^2} \right| + C, \text{ where } C = C_1 - \log |a|$$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Applying these standard formulae, we now obtain some more formulae which
are useful from applications point of view and can be applied directly to evaluate
other integrals.

blocks.label: List
blocks.text: (7) To find the integral $\int \frac{dx}{ax^2 + bx + c}$, we write

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ax^2 + bx + c = a \left[ x^2 + \frac{b}{a}x + \frac{c}{a} \right] = a \left[ \left( x + \frac{b}{2a} \right)^2 + \left( \frac{c}{a} - \frac{b^2}{4a^2} \right) \right]$$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Now, put $x + \frac{b}{2a} = t$ so that $dx = dt$ and writing $\frac{c}{a} - \frac{b^2}{4a^2} = \pm k^2$. We find the

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
integral reduced to the form $\frac{1}{a} \int \frac{dt}{t^2 \pm k^2}$ depending upon the sign of $\left( \frac{c}{a} - \frac{b^2}{4a^2} \right)$
and hence can be evaluated.

blocks.label: List
blocks.text:
(8) To find the integral of the type $\int \frac{dx}{\sqrt{ax^2 + bx + c}}$, proceeding as in (7), we
obtain the integral using the standard formulae.

blocks.label: List
blocks.text:
(9) To find the integral of the type $\int \frac{px + q}{ax^2 + bx + c} dx$, where $p, q, a, b, c$ are
constants, we are to find real numbers A, B such that

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$px + q = \mathrm{A} \frac{d}{dx}(ax^2 + bx + c) + \mathrm{B} = \mathrm{A} (2ax + b) + \mathrm{B}$$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
To determine A and B, we equate from both sides the coefficients of $x$ and the
constant terms. A and B are thus obtained and hence the integral is reduced to
one of the known forms.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
(10) For the evaluation of the integral of the type $\int \frac{(px+q) dx}{\sqrt{ax^2+bx+c}}$, we proceed
as in (9) and transform the integral into known standard forms.
Let us illustrate the above methods by some examples.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text: Example 8 Find the following integrals:

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: (i) $\int \frac{dx}{x^2 - 16}$ (ii) $\int \frac{dx}{\sqrt{2x - x^2}}$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Solution

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: (i) We have $\int \frac{dx}{x^2-16} = \int \frac{dx}{x^2-4^2} = \frac{1}{8} \log \left| \frac{x-4}{x+4} \right| + C$ [by 7.4 (1)]

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: (ii) $\int \frac{dx}{\sqrt{2x-x^2}} = \int \frac{dx}{\sqrt{1-(x-1)^2}}$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Put $x - 1 = t$. Then $dx = dt$.

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
Therefore, $\int \frac{dx}{\sqrt{2x-x^2}} = \int \frac{dt}{\sqrt{1-t^2}} = \sin^{-1} (t) + \text{C}$ [by 7.4 (5)]

$= \sin^{-1} (x-1) + \text{C}$

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 9 Find the following integrals :

(i) $\int \frac{dx}{x^2 - 6x + 13}$ (ii) $\int \frac{dx}{3x^2 + 13x - 10}$ (iii) $\int \frac{dx}{\sqrt{5x^2 - 2x}}$

Solution

(i) We have $x^2 - 6x + 13 = x^2 - 6x + 3^2 - 3^2 + 13 = (x - 3)^2 + 4$

So, $\int \frac{dx}{x^2 - 6x + 13} = \int \frac{1}{(x - 3)^2 + 2^2} dx$

Let $x - 3 = t$. Then $dx = dt$

Therefore, $\int \frac{dx}{x^2 - 6x + 13} = \int \frac{dt}{t^2 + 2^2} = \frac{1}{2} \tan^{-1} \frac{t}{2} + C$ [by 7.4 (3)]

$= \frac{1}{2} \tan^{-1} \frac{x - 3}{2} + C$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: (ii) The given integral is of the form 7.4 (7). We write the denominator of the integrand,

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
$$3x^2 + 13x - 10 = 3\left(x^2 + \frac{13x}{3} - \frac{10}{3}\right)$$

$$= 3\left[\left(x + \frac{13}{6}\right)^2 - \left(\frac{17}{6}\right)^2\right] \text{ (completing the square)}$$

blocks.label: Equation

blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: 7.5 Integration by Partial Fractions

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Recall that a rational function is defined as the ratio of two polynomials in the form


$\frac{\mathrm{P}(x)}{\mathrm{Q}(x)}$, where $\mathrm{P}$ $(x)$ and $\mathrm{Q}(x)$ are polynomials in $x$ and $\mathrm{Q}(x) \neq 0$. If the degree of $\mathrm{P}(x)$


is less than the degree of $\mathrm{Q}(x)$, then the rational function is called proper, otherwise, it


is called improper. The improper rational functions can be reduced to the proper rational

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: functions by long division process. Thus, if $\frac{\mathrm{P}(x)}{\mathrm{Q}(x)}$ is improper, then $\frac{\mathrm{P}(x)}{\mathrm{Q}(x)} = \mathrm{T}(x) + \frac{\mathrm{P}_1(x)}{\mathrm{Q}(x)}$,

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: where $T(x)$ is a polynomial in $x$ and $\frac{P_1(x)}{Q(x)}$ is a proper rational function. As we know

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
how to integrate polynomials, the integration of any rational function is reduced to the
integration of a proper rational function. The rational functions which we shall consider
here for integration purposes will be those whose denominators can be factorised into

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: linear and quadratic factors. Assume that we want to evaluate $\int \frac{\mathrm{P}(x)}{\mathrm{Q}(x)} \, dx$, where $\frac{\mathrm{P}(x)}{\mathrm{Q}(x)}$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
is proper rational function. It is always possible to write the integrand as a sum of
simpler rational functions by a method called partial fraction decomposition. After this,
the integration can be carried out easily using the already known methods. The following
Table 7.2 indicates the types of simpler partial fractions that are to be associated with
various kind of rational functions.

blocks.label: Table-caption
blocks.text: Table 7.2

blocks.label: Table
blocks.text:

1. $\frac{px+q}{(x-a)(x-b)}$, $a \neq b$ $\frac{A}{x-a} + \frac{B}{x-b}$
2. $\frac{px+q}{(x-a)^2}$ $\frac{A}{x-a} + \frac{B}{(x-a)^2}$
3. $\frac{px^2+qx+r}{(x-a)(x-b)(x-c)}$ $\frac{A}{x-a} + \frac{B}{x-b} + \frac{C}{x-c}$
4. $\frac{px^2+qx+r}{(x-a)^2(x-b)}$ $\frac{A}{x-a} + \frac{B}{(x-a)^2} + \frac{C}{x-b}$
5. $\frac{px^2+qx+r}{(x-a)(x^2+bx+c)}$ $\frac{A}{x-a} + \frac{Bx+C}{x^2+bx+c}$,
where $x^2+bx+c$ cannot be factorised further

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: In the above table, A, B and C are real numbers to be determined suitably.

Solution The integrand is of the type as given in Table 7.2 (4). We write

$$\frac{3x-2}{(x+1)^{2}(x+3)} = \frac{A}{x+1} + \frac{B}{(x+1)^{2}} + \frac{C}{x+3}$$

So that $3x-2 = A(x+1)(x+3) + B(x+3) + C(x+1)^{2}$

Comparing coefficient of $x^{2}$, $x$ and constant term on both sides, we get

$$\frac{3x-2}{(x+1)^{2}(x+3)} = \frac{11}{4(x+1)} - \frac{5}{2(x+1)^{2}} - \frac{11}{4(x+3)}$$

Therefore, $$\int \frac{3x-2}{(x+1)^{2}(x+3)} = \frac{11}{4} \int \frac{dx}{x+1} - \frac{5}{2} \int \frac{dx}{(x+1)^{2}} - \frac{11}{4} \int \frac{dx}{x+3}$$
$$= \frac{11}{4} \log |x+1| + \frac{5}{2(x+1)} - \frac{11}{4} \log |x+3| + C$$
$$= \frac{11}{4} \log \left| \frac{x+1}{x+3} \right| + \frac{5}{2(x+1)} + C$$

blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: 7.6 Integration by Parts

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
In this section, we describe one more method of integration, that is found quite useful in
integrating products of functions.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
If $u$ and $v$ are any two differentiable functions of a single variable $x$ (say). Then, by
the product rule of differentiation, we have

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \frac{d}{dx}(uv) = u \frac{dv}{dx} + v \frac{du}{dx} $$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Integrating both sides, we get

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$uv = \int u \frac{dv}{dx} dx + \int v \frac{du}{dx} dx$$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
or
$$ \int u \frac{dv}{dx} dx = uv - \int v \frac{du}{dx} dx \qquad \dots (1) $$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Let $u = f(x)$ and $\frac{dv}{dx} = g(x)$. Then

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \frac{du}{dx} = f'(x) \text{ and } v = \int g(x) \, dx $$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Therefore, expression (1) can be rewritten as

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \int f(x) g(x) dx = f(x) \int g(x) dx - \int [ \int g(x) dx ] f'(x) dx $$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: i.e., $\int f(x) g(x) d x=f(x) \int g(x) d x-\int\left[f^{\prime}(x) \int g(x) d x\right] d x$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
If we take $f$ as the first function and $g$ as the second function, then this formula
may be stated as follows:

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
“The integral of the product of two functions = (first function) $\times$ (integral
of the second function) – Integral of [(differential coefficient of the first function)
$\times$ (integral of the second function)]”

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text: Example 17 Find $\int x \cos x \, dx$

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 17 Find $\int x \cos x \, dx$

Solution Put $f(x) = x$ (first function) and $g(x) = \cos x$ (second function).
Then, integration by parts gives

$$\int x \cos x \, dx = x \int \cos x \, dx - \int [\frac{d}{dx}(x) \int \cos x \, dx] \, dx$$
$$= x \sin x - \int \sin x \, dx = x \sin x + \cos x + C$$

Suppose, we take $f(x) = \cos x$ and $g(x) = x$. Then

$$\int x \cos x \, dx = \cos x \int x \, dx - \int [\frac{d}{dx}(\cos x) \int x \, dx] \, dx$$
$$= (\cos x) \frac{x^2}{2} + \int \sin x \frac{x^2}{2} \, dx$$

Thus, it shows that the integral $\int x \cos x \, dx$ is reduced to the comparatively more
complicated integral having more power of $x$. Therefore, the proper choice of the first
function and the second function is significant.

blocks.label: Sub-section-title
blocks.text: Remarks

blocks.label: List
blocks.text:
(i) It is worth mentioning that integration by parts is not applicable to product of
functions in all cases. For instance, the method does not work for $\int \sqrt{x} \sin x \, dx$.
The reason is that there does not exist any function whose derivative is
$\sqrt{x} \sin x$.

(ii) Observe that while finding the integral of the second function, we did not add
any constant of integration. If we write the integral of the second function $\cos x$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: as $\sin x + k$, where $k$ is any constant, then

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
$$\int x \cos x \, dx = x (\sin x + k) - \int (\sin x + k) \, dx$$
$$= x (\sin x + k) - \int (\sin x \, dx - \int k \, dx$$
$$= x (\sin x + k) - \cos x - kx + \text{C} = x \sin x + \cos x + \text{C}$$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
This shows that adding a constant to the integral of the second function is
superfluous so far as the final result is concerned while applying the method of
integration by parts.

blocks.label: List
blocks.text:
(iii) Usually, if any function is a power of $x$ or a polynomial in $x$, then we take it as the
first function. However, in cases where other function is inverse trigonometric
function or logarithmic function, then we take them as first function.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 18 Find $\int \log x \, dx$

Solution To start with, we are unable to guess a function whose derivative is $\log x$. We
take $\log x$ as the first function and the constant function $1$ as the second function. Then,
the integral of the second function is $x$.

Hence, $$\int (\log x.1) \, dx = \log x \int 1 \, dx - \int [\frac{d}{dx} (\log x) \int 1 \, dx] \, dx$$
$$= (\log x) \cdot x - \int \frac{1}{x} x \, dx = x \log x - x + C.$$

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 19 Find $\int x e^x dx$

Solution Take first function as $x$ and second function as $e^x$. The integral of the second
function is $e^x$.

Therefore, $$\int x e^x dx = x e^x - \int 1 \cdot e^x dx = x e^x - e^x + \text{C}.$$

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 20 Find $\int \frac{x \sin^{-1} x}{\sqrt{1-x^2}} dx$


Solution Let first function be $\sin^{-1} x$ and second function be $\frac{x}{\sqrt{1-x^2}}$.


First we find the integral of the second function, i.e., $\int \frac{x dx}{\sqrt{1-x^2}}$.


Put $t = 1 - x^2$. Then $dt = -2x dx$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Put $t=1-x^2$. Then $dt=-2x\ dx$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Therefore, $\int \frac{x \, dx}{\sqrt{1-x^2}} = -\frac{1}{2} \int \frac{dt}{\sqrt{t}} = -\sqrt{t} = -\sqrt{1-x^2}$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
Hence, $\int \frac{x \sin^{-1} x}{\sqrt{1-x^2}} dx = (\sin^{-1} x) \left( -\sqrt{1-x^2} \right) - \int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-x^2}} (-\sqrt{1-x^2}) dx$
$= -\sqrt{1-x^2} \sin^{-1} x + x + C = x - \sqrt{1-x^2} \sin^{-1} x + C$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
**Alternatively**, this integral can also be worked out by making substitution $\sin^{-1}x = \theta$ and
then integrating by parts.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text: Example 21 Find $\int e^x \sin x \, dx$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Solution Take $e^x$ as the first function and $\sin x$ as second function. Then, integrating
by parts, we have

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
$$ \text{I} = \int e^x \sin x \, dx = e^x (-\cos x) + \int e^x \cos x \, dx $$
$$ = -e^x \cos x + \text{I}_1 \text{ (say)} \quad \dots (1) $$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Taking $e^x$ and $\cos x$ as the first and second functions, respectively, in $\mathrm{I}_1$, we get

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$I_1 = e^x \sin x - \int e^x \sin x \, dx$$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
Substituting the value of $I_1$ in (1), we get
$$I = -e^x \cos x + e^x \sin x - I \text{ or } 2I = e^x (\sin x - \cos x)$$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Hence, $I = \int e^x \sin x \, dx = \frac{e^x}{2} (\sin x - \cos x) + C$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
**Alternatively**, above integral can also be determined by taking $\sin x$ as the first function
and $e^x$ the second function.

blocks.label: Sub-section-title
blocks.text: 7.6.1 Integral of the type $\int e^x [ f(x) + f'(x) ] dx$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
We have
$$ \begin{aligned} \mathrm{I} &= \int e^x [ f(x) + f'(x) ] dx = \int e^x f(x) dx + \int e^x f'(x) dx \\ &= \mathrm{I}_1 + \int e^x f'(x) dx, \text{ where } \mathrm{I}_1 = \int e^x f(x) dx \end{aligned} \quad \dots (1) $$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Taking $f(x)$ and $e^x$ as the first function and second function, respectively, in $\mathrm{I}_1$ and
integrating it by parts, we have $\mathrm{I}_1 = f(x) e^x - \int f'(x) e^x dx + \mathrm{C}$
Substituting $\mathrm{I}_1$ in (1), we get

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$I = e^x f(x) - \int f'(x) e^x dx + \int e^x f'(x) dx + C = e^x f(x) + C$$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Thus, $\int e^x [f(x) + f'(x)] dx = e^x f(x) + C$

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text: Example 22 Find (i) $\int e^x(\tan^{-1}x + \frac{1}{1+x^2}) dx$ (ii) $\int \frac{(x^2 + 1) e^x}{(x + 1)^2} dx$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Solution

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: (i) We have $I = \int e^x (\tan^{-1} x + \frac{1}{1+x^2}) dx$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Consider $f(x) = \tan^{-1}x$, then $f'(x) = \frac{1}{1+x^2}$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Thus, the given integrand is of the form $e^x [f(x) + f'(x)]$.

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Therefore, $I = \int e^x (\tan^{-1} x + \frac{1}{1+x^2}) dx = e^x \tan^{-1} x + C$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: (ii) We have $I = \int \frac{(x^2 + 1) e^x}{(x + 1)^2} dx = \int e^x [\frac{x^2 - 1 + 1 + 1}{(x + 1)^2}] dx$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$= \int e^x \left[ \frac{x^2 - 1}{(x + 1)^2} + \frac{2}{(x + 1)^2} \right] dx = \int e^x \left[ \frac{x - 1}{x + 1} + \frac{2}{(x + 1)^2} \right] dx$$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Consider $f(x)=\frac{x-1}{x+1}$, then $f'(x)=\frac{2}{(x+1)^{2}}$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Thus, the given integrand is of the form $e^x [f(x) + f'(x)]$.

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Therefore, $\int \frac{x^2+1}{(x+1)^2} e^x dx = \frac{x-1}{x+1} e^x + C$

blocks.label: Sub-section-title
blocks.text: 7.6.2 Integrals of some more types

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Here, we discuss some special types of standard integrals based on the technique of
integration by parts :

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: (i) $\int \sqrt{x^2 - a^2} dx$ (ii) $\int \sqrt{x^2 + a^2} dx$ (iii) $\int \sqrt{a^2 - x^2} dx$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: (i) Let $I = \int \sqrt{x^2 - a^2} dx$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Taking constant function 1 as the second function and integrating by parts, we
have

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$I = x \sqrt{x^2 - a^2} - \int \frac{1}{2} \frac{2x}{\sqrt{x^2 - a^2}} x \, dx$$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ = x \sqrt{x^2 - a^2} - \int \frac{x^2}{\sqrt{x^2 - a^2}} dx = x \sqrt{x^2 - a^2} - \int \frac{x^2 - a^2 + a^2}{\sqrt{x^2 - a^2}} dx $$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ = x \sqrt{x^2 - a^2} - \int \sqrt{x^2 - a^2} \, dx - a^2 \int \frac{dx}{\sqrt{x^2 - a^2}} $$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ = x \sqrt{x^2 - a^2} - \mathrm{I} - a^2 \int \frac{dx}{\sqrt{x^2 - a^2}} $$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: or $2\mathrm{I} = x\sqrt{x^2 - a^2} - a^2 \int \frac{dx}{\sqrt{x^2 - a^2}}$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: or $$ \mathbf{I} = \int \sqrt{x^2 - a^2} \, dx = \frac{x}{2} \sqrt{x^2 - a^2} - \frac{a^2}{2} \log \left| x + \sqrt{x^2 - a^2} \right| + \mathbf{C} $$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Similarly, integrating other two integrals by parts, taking constant function 1 as the
second function, we get

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: (ii) $\int \sqrt{x^2 + a^2} dx = \frac{1}{2} x \sqrt{x^2 + a^2} + \frac{a^2}{2} \log \left| x + \sqrt{x^2 + a^2} \right| + C$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: (iii) $\int \sqrt{a^2 - x^2} dx = \frac{1}{2} x \sqrt{a^2 - x^2} + \frac{a^2}{2} \sin^{-1} \frac{x}{a} + C$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
**Alternatively**, integrals (i), (ii) and (iii) can also be found by making trigonometric
substitution $x = a \sec \theta$ in (i), $x = a \tan \theta$ in (ii) and $x = a \sin \theta$ in (iii) respectively.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 23 Find $\int \sqrt{x^2 + 2x + 5} dx$

Solution Note that

$$\int \sqrt{x^2 + 2x + 5} dx = \int \sqrt{(x+1)^2 + 4} dx$$

Put $x + 1 = y$, so that $dx = dy$. Then

$$\int \sqrt{x^2 + 2x + 5} dx = \int \sqrt{y^2 + 2^2} dy$$

$$= \frac{1}{2} y \sqrt{y^2 + 4} + \frac{4}{2} \log \left| y + \sqrt{y^2 + 4} \right| + C \quad \text{[using 7.6.2 (ii)]}$$

$$= \frac{1}{2} (x + 1) \sqrt{x^2 + 2x + 5} + 2 \log \left| x + 1 + \sqrt{x^2 + 2x + 5} \right| + C$$

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 24 Find $\int \sqrt{3-2x-x^2} dx$

Solution Note that $\int \sqrt{3-2x-x^2} dx = \int \sqrt{4-(x+1)^2} dx$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Put $x + 1 = y$ so that $dx = dy$.

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
Thus $$\int \sqrt{3-2x-x^2} \, dx = \int \sqrt{4-y^2} \, dy$$
$$= \frac{1}{2} y \sqrt{4-y^2} + \frac{4}{2} \sin^{-1} \frac{y}{2} + \text{C} \qquad [\text{using 7.6.2 (iii)}]$$
$$= \frac{1}{2} (x+1) \sqrt{3-2x-x^2} + 2 \sin^{-1} \left( \frac{x+1}{2} \right) + \text{C}$$

blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: 7.7 Definite Integral

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
In the previous sections, we have studied about the indefinite integrals and discussed
few methods of finding them including integrals of some special functions. In this
section, we shall study what is called definite integral of a function. The definite integral

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: has a unique value. A definite integral is denoted by $\int_{a}^{b} f(x) dx$, where $a$ is called the

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
lower limit of the integral and $b$ is called the upper limit of the integral. The definite
integral is introduced either as the limit of a sum or if it has an anti derivative $\mathrm{F}$ in the
interval $[a, b]$, then its value is the difference between the values of $\mathrm{F}$ at the end
points, i.e., $\mathrm{F}(b) - \mathrm{F}(a)$.

blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: 7.8 Fundamental Theorem of Calculus

blocks.label: Sub-section-title
blocks.text: 7.8.1 Area function

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
We have defined $\int_{a}^{b} f(x) dx$ as the area of
the region bounded by the curve $y = f(x)$,
the ordinates $x = a$ and $x = b$ and $x$-axis. Let $x$
be a given point in $[a, b]$. Then $\int_{a}^{x} f(x) dx$
represents the area of the light shaded region
in Fig 7.1 [Here it is assumed that $f(x) > 0$ for
$x \in [a, b]$, the assertion made below is
equally true for other functions as well].
The area of this shaded region depends upon
the value of $x$.

blocks.label: Image-caption
blocks.text: Fig 7.1

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
In other words, the area of this shaded region is a function of $x$. We denote this
function of $x$ by $\mathrm{A}(x)$. We call the function $\mathrm{A}(x)$ as $Area\ function$ and is given by

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \mathbf{A}(x) = \int_{a}^{x} f(x) dx \qquad \dots (1) $$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Based on this definition, the two basic fundamental theorems have been given.
However, we only state them as their proofs are beyond the scope of this text book.

blocks.label: Sub-section-title
blocks.text: 7.8.2 First fundamental theorem of integral calculus

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Theorem 1 Let $f$ be a continuous function on the closed interval $[a, b]$ and let $\mathrm{A}(x)$ be
the area function. Then $\mathrm{A}^{\prime}(\boldsymbol{x})=f(\boldsymbol{x})$, for all $\boldsymbol{x} \in[\boldsymbol{a}, \boldsymbol{b}]$.

blocks.label: Sub-section-title
blocks.text: 7.8.3 Second fundamental theorem of integral calculus

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
We state below an important theorem which enables us to evaluate definite integrals
by making use of anti derivative.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Theorem 2 Let $f$ be continuous function defined on the closed interval $[a, b]$ and $\mathrm{F}$ be

an anti derivative of $f$. Then $\int_{a}^{b} f(x) d x=[\mathbf{F}(x)]_{a}^{b}=\mathbf{F}(b)-\mathbf{F}(a)$.

blocks.label: Sub-section-title
blocks.text: Remarks

blocks.label: List
blocks.text:
(i) In words, the Theorem 2 tells us that $\int_{a}^{b} f(x) \, dx = (\text{value of the anti derivative F})$
of $f$ at the upper limit $b$ – value of the same anti derivative at the lower limit $a$).

(ii) This theorem is very useful, because it gives us a method of calculating the
definite integral more easily, without calculating the limit of a sum.

(iii) The crucial operation in evaluating a definite integral is that of finding a function
whose derivative is equal to the integrand. This strengthens the relationship
between differentiation and integration.

(iv) In $\int_{a}^{b} f(x) \, dx$, the function $f$ needs to be well defined and continuous in $[a, b]$.

For instance, the consideration of definite integral $\int_{-2}^{3} x(x^{2} - 1)^{\frac{1}{2}} \, dx$ is erroneous

since the function $f$ expressed by $f(x) = x(x^{2} - 1)^{\frac{1}{2}}$ is not defined in a portion
$-1 < x < 1$ of the closed interval $[-2, 3]$.

Steps for calculating $\int_{a}^{b} f(x) \, dx$.

(i) Find the indefinite integral $\int f(x) \, dx$. Let this be $F(x)$. There is no need to keep
integration constant C because if we consider $F(x) + C$ instead of $F(x)$, we get
$$\int_{a}^{b} f(x) \, dx = [F(x) + C]_{a}^{b} = [F(b) + C] - [F(a) + C] = F(b) - F(a).$$
Thus, the arbitrary constant disappears in evaluating the value of the definite
integral.

(ii) Evaluate $F(b) - F(a) = [F(x)]_{a}^{b}$, which is the value of $\int_{a}^{b} f(x) \, dx$.

We now consider some examples

blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: 7.9 Evaluation of Definite Integrals by Substitution

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
In the previous sections, we have discussed several methods for finding the indefinite
integral. One of the important methods for finding the indefinite integral is the method
of substitution.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: To evaluate $\int_{a}^{b} f(x) dx$, by substitution, the steps could be as follows:

blocks.label: List
blocks.text:
1. Consider the integral without limits and substitute, $y = f(x)$ or $x = g(y)$ to reduce
the given integral to a known form.
2. Integrate the new integrand with respect to the new variable without mentioning
the constant of integration.
3. Resubstitute for the new variable and write the answer in terms of the original
variable.
4. Find the values of answers obtained in (3) at the given limits of integral and find
the difference of the values at the upper and lower limits.

blocks.label: Infobox
blocks.text:
Note In order to quicken this method, we can proceed as follows: After
performing steps 1, and 2, there is no need of step 3. Here, the integral will be kept
in the new variable itself, and the limits of the integral will accordingly be changed,
so that we can perform the last step.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Let us illustrate this by examples.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
**Alternatively**, first we transform the integral and then evaluate the transformed integral
with new limits.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Let $t = x^5 + 1$. Then $dt = 5 \ x^4 \ dx$.
Note that, when $x = -1$, $t = 0$ and when $x = 1$, $t = 2$
Thus, as $x$ varies from $-1$ to $1$, $t$ varies from $0$ to $2$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Thus, as $x$ varies from $-1$ to $1$, $t$ varies from $0$ to $2$

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text: Example 27 Evaluate $\int_{0}^{1} \frac{\tan^{-1} x}{1+x^{2}} dx$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Solution Let $t = \tan^{-1}x$, then $dt = \frac{1}{1 + x^2} dx$. The new limits are, when $x = 0$, $t = 0$ and

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: when $x=1$, $t=\frac{\pi}{4}$. Thus, as $x$ varies from 0 to 1, $t$ varies from 0 to $\frac{\pi}{4}$.

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Therefore $\int_{0}^{1} \frac{\tan^{-1} x}{1+x^{2}} dx = \int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{4}} t dt \left[ \frac{t^{2}}{2} \right]_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{4}} = \frac{1}{2} \left[ \frac{\pi^{2}}{16} - 0 \right] = \frac{\pi^{2}}{32}$

blocks.text: 7.10 Some Properties of Definite Integrals

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
We list below some important properties of definite integrals. These will be useful in
evaluating the definite integrals more easily.

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
$\mathbf{P}_{0}: \quad \int_{a}^{b} f(x) d x=\int_{a}^{b} f(t) d t$

$\mathbf{P}_{1}: \quad \int_{a}^{b} f(x) d x=-\int_{b}^{a} f(x) d x$. In particular, $\int_{a}^{a} f(x) d x=0$

$\mathbf{P}_{2}: \quad \int_{a}^{b} f(x) d x=\int_{a}^{c} f(x) d x+\int_{c}^{b} f(x) d x$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \mathbf{P}_3 : \quad \int_a^b f(x) dx = \int_a^b f(a+b-x) dx $$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \mathbf{P}_4 : \quad \int_0^a f(x) dx = \int_0^a f(a-x) dx $$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: (Note that $\mathrm{P}_4$ is a particular case of $\mathrm{P}_3$)

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \mathbf{P_5} : \quad \int_0^{2a} f(x) dx = \int_0^a f(x) dx + \int_0^a f(2a-x) dx $$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
$$ \mathbf{P}_6 : \quad \int_0^{2a} f(x) dx = 2 \int_0^a f(x) dx, \text{if } f(2a-x) = f(x) \quad \text{and} $$
$$ 0 \text{ if } f(2a-x) = -f(x) $$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $\mathbf{P}_{7}:$ (i) $\int_{-a}^{a} f(x) d x=2 \int_{0}^{a} f(x) d x$, if $f$ is an even function, i.e., if $f(-x)=f(x)$.

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: (ii) $\int_{-a}^{a} f(x)dx = 0$, if $f$ is an odd function, i.e., if $f(-x) = -f(x)$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: We give the proofs of these properties one by one.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: **Proof of $\mathbf{P}_0$** It follows directly by making the substitution $x = t$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
**Proof of $\mathbf{P_1}$** Let $\mathrm{F}$ be anti derivative of $f$. Then, by the second fundamental theorem of
calculus, we have $\int_a^b f(x)dx = \mathrm{F}(b) - \mathrm{F}(a) = -[\mathrm{F}(a) - \mathrm{F}(b)] = -\int_b^a f(x)dx$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Here, we observe that, if $a=b$, then $\int_{a}^{a} f(x) d x=0$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: **Proof of $\mathbf{P_2}$** Let F be anti derivative of $f$. Then

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \int_{a}^{b} f(x) \, dx = \mathrm{F}(b) - \mathrm{F}(a) \qquad \dots (1) $$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \int_{a}^{c} f(x) \, dx = \mathrm{F}(c) - \mathrm{F}(a) \qquad \dots (2) $$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: and $\int_{c}^{b} f(x) \, dx = \mathrm{F}(b) - \mathrm{F}(c)$ \hfill ... (3)

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Adding (2) and (3), we get $\int_{a}^{c} f(x) dx + \int_{c}^{b} f(x) dx = \mathrm{F}(b) - \mathrm{F}(a) = \int_{a}^{b} f(x) dx$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: This proves the property $\mathrm{P}_2$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
**Proof of $\mathbf{P}_3$** Let $t = a + b - x$. Then $dt = - dx$. When $x = a, t = b$ and when $x = b, t = a$.
Therefore

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \int_{a}^{b} f(x) dx = -\int_{b}^{a} f(a+b-t) dt $$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ = \int_{a}^{b} f(a+b-t) dt \quad (\text{by } \mathrm{P}_1) $$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ = \int_{a}^{b} f(a+b-x) \, dx \text{ by } \mathrm{P}_{0} $$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
**Proof of** $\mathbf{P}_4$ Put $t = a - x$. Then $dt = - dx$. When $x = 0$, $t = a$ and when $x = a$, $t = 0$. Now
proceed as in $\mathrm{P}_3$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: **Proof of P$_5$** Using $\mathrm{P}_2$, we have $\int_0^{2a} f(x) \, dx = \int_0^a f(x) \, dx + \int_a^{2a} f(x) \, dx$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Let $t = 2a - x$ in the second integral on the right hand side. Then
$dt = - dx$. When $x = a$, $t = a$ and when $x = 2a$, $t = 0$. Also $x = 2a - t$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Therefore, the second integral becomes

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Hence $\int_{0}^{2a} f(x) dx = \int_{0}^{a} f(x) dx + \int_{0}^{a} f(2a - x) dx$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: **Proof of P$_6$** Using $\mathrm{P}_5$, we have $\int_0^{2a} f(x) \, dx = \int_0^a f(x) \, dx + \int_0^a f(2a-x) \, dx \quad ... (1)$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Now, if $f(2a - x) = f(x)$, then (1) becomes

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: and if $f(2a - x) = -f(x)$, then (1) becomes

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Proof of $\mathbf{P}_7$ Using $\mathbf{P}_2$, we have

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \int_{-a}^{a} f(x) dx = \int_{-a}^{0} f(x) dx + \int_{0}^{a} f(x) dx . \text{ Then} $$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
Let $t = -x$ in the first integral on the right hand side.
$dt = -dx$. When $x = -a$, $t = a$ and when
$x = 0$, $t = 0$. Also $x = -t$.

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Therefore $$\int_{-a}^{a} f(x) \, dx = -\int_{a}^{0} f(-t) \, dt + \int_{0}^{a} f(x) \, dx$$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ = \int_{0}^{a} f(-x) \, dx + \int_{0}^{a} f(x) \, dx \qquad (\text{by } \mathrm{P}_{0}) \quad \dots (1) $$

blocks.label: List
blocks.text:
(i) Now, if $f$ is an even function, then $f(-x) = f(x)$ and so (1) becomes

$$\int_{-a}^{a} f(x) dx = \int_{0}^{a} f(x) dx + \int_{0}^{a} f(x) dx = 2 \int_{0}^{a} f(x) dx$$

(ii) If $f$ is an odd function, then $f(-x) = -f(x)$ and so (1) becomes

$$\int_{-a}^{a} f(x) dx = -\int_{0}^{a} f(x) dx + \int_{0}^{a} f(x) dx = 0$$

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text: Example 28 Evaluate $\int_{-1}^{2} \left| x^3 - x \right| dx$

blocks.label: Answer
blocks.text:
Solution We note that $x^3 - x \geq 0$ on $[-1, 0]$ and $x^3 - x \leq 0$ on $[0, 1]$ and that
$x^3 - x \geq 0$ on $[1, 2]$. So by $\text{P}_2$ we write

$$ \int_{-1}^2 \left| x^3 - x \right| dx = \int_{-1}^0 (x^3 - x) dx + \int_0^1 - (x^3 - x) dx + \int_1^2 (x^3 - x) dx $$

$$ = \int_{-1}^0 (x^3 - x) dx + \int_0^1 (x - x^3) dx + \int_1^2 (x^3 - x) dx $$

$$ = \left[ \frac{x^4}{4} - \frac{x^2}{2} \right]_{-1}^0 + \left[ \frac{x^2}{2} - \frac{x^4}{4} \right]_0^1 + \left[ \frac{x^4}{4} - \frac{x^2}{2} \right]_1^2 $$

$$ = -\left( \frac{1}{4} - \frac{1}{2} \right) + \left( \frac{1}{2} - \frac{1}{4} \right) + (4 - 2) - \left( \frac{1}{4} - \frac{1}{2} \right) $$

$$ = -\frac{1}{4} + \frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{2} - \frac{1}{4} + 2 - \frac{1}{4} + \frac{1}{2} = \frac{3}{2} - \frac{3}{4} + 2 = \frac{11}{4} $$

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 29 Evaluate $\int_{\frac{-\pi}{4}}^{\frac{\pi}{4}} \sin^2 x \, dx$


Solution We observe that $\sin^2 x$ is an even function. Therefore, by $\text{P}_7$ (i), we get


$$ \int_{\frac{-\pi}{4}}^{\frac{\pi}{4}} \sin^2 x \, dx = 2 \int_0^{\frac{\pi}{4}} \sin^2 x \, dx $$


$$ = 2 \int_0^{\frac{\pi}{4}} \frac{(1 - \cos 2x)}{2} \, dx = \int_0^{\frac{\pi}{4}} (1 - \cos 2x) \, dx $$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ = \left[ x - \frac{1}{2} \sin 2x \right]_0^{\frac{\pi}{4}} = \left( \frac{\pi}{4} - \frac{1}{2} \sin \frac{\pi}{2} \right) - 0 = \frac{\pi}{4} - \frac{1}{2} $$

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text: Example 30 Evaluate $\int_{0}^{\pi} \frac{x \sin x}{1 + \cos^2 x} dx$

blocks.label: Answer
blocks.text: Solution Let $I = \int_{0}^{\pi} \frac{x \sin x}{1 + \cos^2 x} dx$. Then, by $P_4$, we have

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ I = \int_{0}^{\pi} \frac{(\pi - x) \sin (\pi - x) dx}{1 + \cos^2 (\pi - x)} $$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ = \int_{0}^{\pi} \frac{(\pi - x) \sin x \, dx}{1 + \cos^2 x} = \pi \int_{0}^{\pi} \frac{\sin x \, dx}{1 + \cos^2 x} - \mathrm{I} $$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: or $2 I = \pi \int_{0}^{\pi} \frac{\sin x \, dx}{1 + \cos^2 x}$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: or $I = \frac{\pi}{2} \int_{0}^{\pi} \frac{\sin x \, dx}{1 + \cos^2 x}$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Put $\cos x = t$ so that $-\sin x \, dx = dt$. When $x = 0$, $t = 1$ and when $x = \pi$, $t = -1$.
Therefore, (by $\mathrm{P}_1$) we get

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
$$I = \frac{-\pi}{2} \int_{-1}^{-1} \frac{dt}{1+t^2} = \frac{\pi}{2} \int_{-1}^{1} \frac{dt}{1+t^2}$$

$$= \pi \int_{0}^{1} \frac{dt}{1+t^2} \text{ (by P}_7\text{, since } \frac{1}{1+t^2} \text{ is even function)}$$

$$= \pi \left[ \tan^{-1} t \right]_0^1 = \pi \left[ \tan^{-1} 1 - \tan^{-1} 0 \right] = \pi \left[ \frac{\pi}{4} - 0 \right] = \frac{\pi^2}{4}$$

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 31 Evaluate $\int_{-1}^{1} \sin^{5} x \cos^{4} x \, dx$


Solution Let $I = \int_{-1}^{1} \sin^{5} x \cos^{4} x \, dx$. Let $f(x) = \sin^{5} x \cos^{4} x$. Then


$$f(-x) = \sin^{5}(-x) \cos^{4}(-x) = -\sin^{5} x \cos^{4} x = -f(x), \text{ i.e., } f \text{ is an odd function.}$$
Therefore, by $\text{P}_{7}$ (ii), $I = 0$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Adding (1) and (2), we get

blocks.label: Question
blocks.text: Example 33 Evaluate $\int_{\frac{\pi}{6}}^{\frac{\pi}{3}} \frac{dx}{1 + \sqrt{\tan x}}$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Solution Let $I = \int_{\frac{\pi}{6}}^{\frac{\pi}{3}} \frac{dx}{1 + \sqrt{\tan x}} = \int_{\frac{\pi}{6}}^{\frac{\pi}{3}} \frac{\sqrt{\cos x} \, dx}{\sqrt{\cos x} + \sqrt{\sin x}}$ ... (1)

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
Then, by $P_3$
$$I = \int_{\frac{\pi}{6}}^{\frac{\pi}{3}} \frac{\sqrt{\cos \left( \frac{\pi}{3} + \frac{\pi}{6} - x \right)} dx}{\sqrt{\cos \left( \frac{\pi}{3} + \frac{\pi}{6} - x \right)} + \sqrt{\sin \left( \frac{\pi}{3} + \frac{\pi}{6} - x \right)}}$$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ = \int_{\frac{\pi}{6}}^{\frac{\pi}{3}} \frac{\sqrt{\sin x}}{\sqrt{\sin x} + \sqrt{\cos x}} \, dx \qquad \dots (2) $$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Adding (1) and (2), we get

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$2\mathrm{I} = \int_{\frac{\pi}{6}}^{\frac{\pi}{3}} dx = [x]_{\frac{\pi}{6}}^{\frac{\pi}{3}} = \frac{\pi}{3} - \frac{\pi}{6} = \frac{\pi}{6} \text{ . Hence } \mathrm{I} = \frac{\pi}{12}$$

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text: Example 34 Evaluate $\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \log \sin x \, dx$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Solution Let $I = \int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \log \sin x \, dx$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Then, by $\text{P}_4$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$I = \int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \log \sin \left( \frac{\pi}{2} - x \right) dx = \int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \log \cos x \, dx$$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Adding the two values of I, we get

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
$$2I = \int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}} (\log \sin x + \log \cos x) dx$$

$$= \int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}} (\log \sin x \cos x + \log 2 - \log 2) dx \text{ (by adding and subtracting } \log 2)$$

$$= \int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \log \sin 2x dx - \int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \log 2 dx \quad \text{(Why?)}$$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Put $2x = t$ in the first integral. Then $2 \ dx = dt$, when $x = 0$, $t = 0$ and when $x = \frac{\pi}{2}$,
$t = \pi$.

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
Therefore $2\mathrm{I} = \frac{1}{2} \int_{0}^{\pi} \log \sin t \, dt - \frac{\pi}{2} \log 2$

$= \frac{2}{2} \int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \log \sin t \, dt - \frac{\pi}{2} \log 2$ [by $\mathrm{P}_{6}$ as $\sin (\pi - t) = \sin t$)

$= \int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \log \sin x \, dx - \frac{\pi}{2} \log 2$ (by changing variable $t$ to $x$)

$= \mathrm{I} - \frac{\pi}{2} \log 2$

Hence $\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \log \sin x \, dx = \frac{-\pi}{2} \log 2$.

Example 38 Find $\int \left[ \log (\log x) + \frac{1}{(\log x)^2} \right] dx$


Solution Let $I = \int \left[ \log (\log x) + \frac{1}{(\log x)^2} \right] dx$


$= \int \log (\log x) dx + \int \frac{1}{(\log x)^2} dx$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
In the first integral, let us take $1$ as the second function. Then integrating it by
parts, we get

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$I = x \log (\log x) - \int \frac{1}{x \log x} x \, dx + \int \frac{dx}{(\log x)^2}$$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ = x \log (\log x) - \int \frac{dx}{\log x} + \int \frac{dx}{(\log x)^2} \qquad \dots (1) $$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Again, consider $\int \frac{dx}{\log x}$, take 1 as the second function and integrate it by parts,

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: we have $\int \frac{dx}{\log x} = \left[ \frac{x}{\log x} - \int x \left\{ -\frac{1}{(\log x)^2} \left( \frac{1}{x} \right) \right\} dx \right]$ \hfill $(2)$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Putting (2) in (1), we get

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$I = x \log (\log x) - \frac{x}{\log x} - \int \frac{dx}{(\log x)^2} + \int \frac{dx}{(\log x)^2} = x \log (\log x) - \frac{x}{\log x} + C$$

blocks.text: Example 39 Find $\int \left[ \sqrt{\cot x} + \sqrt{\tan x} \right] dx$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Solution We have

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$I = \int \left[ \sqrt{\cot x} + \sqrt{\tan x} \right] dx = \int \sqrt{\tan x} (1 + \cot x) dx$$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Put $\tan x = t^2$, so that $\sec^2 x \, dx = 2t \, dt$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: or $$dx = \frac{2t \, dt}{1 + t^4}$$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Then $I = \int t \left( 1 + \frac{1}{t^2} \right) \frac{2t}{(1+t^4)} dt$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$= 2 \int \frac{(t^2 + 1)}{t^4 + 1} dt = 2 \int \frac{\left(1 + \frac{1}{t^2}\right) dt}{\left(t^2 + \frac{1}{t^2}\right)} = 2 \int \frac{\left(1 + \frac{1}{t^2}\right) dt}{\left(t - \frac{1}{t}\right)^2 + 2}$$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Put $t - \frac{1}{t} = y$, so that $\left( 1 + \frac{1}{t^2} \right) dt = dy$. Then

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$I = 2\int \frac{dy}{y^2 + (\sqrt{2})^2} = \sqrt{2} \tan^{-1} \frac{y}{\sqrt{2}} + C = \sqrt{2} \tan^{-1} \frac{\left(t - \frac{1}{t}\right)}{\sqrt{2}} + C$$

blocks.label: Equation

Therefore $\int_{-1}^{\frac{3}{2}} |x \sin \pi x| dx = \int_{-1}^{1} x \sin \pi x dx + \int_{1}^{\frac{3}{2}} -x \sin \pi x dx$
$= \int_{-1}^{1} x \sin \pi x dx - \int_{1}^{\frac{3}{2}} x \sin \pi x dx$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Integrating both integrals on righthand side, we get

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
$$ \int_{-1}^{\frac{3}{2}} |x \sin \pi x| dx = \left[ \frac{-x \cos \pi x}{\pi} + \frac{\sin \pi x}{\pi^2} \right]_{-1}^1 - \left[ \frac{-x \cos \pi x}{\pi} + \frac{\sin \pi x}{\pi^2} \right]_1^3 $$

$$ = \frac{2}{\pi} - \left[ -\frac{1}{\pi^2} - \frac{1}{\pi} \right] = \frac{3}{\pi} + \frac{1}{\pi^2} $$

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 42 Evaluate $\int_{0}^{\pi} \frac{x \, dx}{a^{2} \cos^{2} x + b^{2} \sin^{2} x}$

Solution Let I = $\int_{0}^{\pi} \frac{x \, dx}{a^{2} \cos^{2} x + b^{2} \sin^{2} x} = \int_{0}^{\pi} \frac{(\pi - x) \, dx}{a^{2} \cos^{2} (\pi - x) + b^{2} \sin^{2} (\pi - x)}$ (using $\text{P}_{4}$)

$= \pi \int_{0}^{\pi} \frac{dx}{a^{2} \cos^{2} x + b^{2} \sin^{2} x} - \int_{0}^{\pi} \frac{x \, dx}{a^{2} \cos^{2} x + b^{2} \sin^{2} x}$

$= \pi \int_{0}^{\pi} \frac{dx}{a^{2} \cos^{2} x + b^{2} \sin^{2} x} - \text{I}$

Thus $2\text{I} = \pi \int_{0}^{\pi} \frac{dx}{a^{2} \cos^{2} x + b^{2} \sin^{2} x}$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
or
$$ \mathrm{I} = \frac{\pi}{2} \int_{0}^{\pi} \frac{dx}{a^{2} \cos^{2} x + b^{2} \sin^{2} x} = \frac{\pi}{2} \cdot 2 \int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \frac{dx}{a^{2} \cos^{2} x + b^{2} \sin^{2} x} \text{ (using } \mathrm{P}_{6} \text{)} $$
$$ = \pi \left[ \int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{4}} \frac{dx}{a^{2} \cos^{2} x + b^{2} \sin^{2} x} + \int_{\frac{\pi}{4}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \frac{dx}{a^{2} \cos^{2} x + b^{2} \sin^{2} x} \right] $$
$$ = \pi \left[ \int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{4}} \frac{\sec^{2} x \, dx}{a^{2} + b^{2} \tan^{2} x} + \int_{\frac{\pi}{4}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \frac{\operatorname{cosec}^{2} x \, dx}{a^{2} \cot^{2} x + b^{2}} \right] $$
$$ = \pi \left[ \int_{0}^{1} \frac{dt}{a^{2} + b^{2} t^{2}} - \int_{1}^{0} \frac{du}{a^{2} u^{2} + b^{2}} \right] \text{ ( } put \tan x = t \text{ and } \cot x = u \text{) } $$
$$ = \frac{\pi}{ab} \left[ \tan^{-1} \frac{bt}{a} \right]_{0}^{-1} - \frac{\pi}{ab} \left[ \tan^{-1} \frac{au}{b} \right]_{1}^{0} = \frac{\pi}{ab} \left[ \tan^{-1} \frac{b}{a} + \tan^{-1} \frac{a}{b} \right] = \frac{\pi^{2}}{2ab} $$

Summary

$\diamond$ Integration is the inverse process of differentiation. In the differential calculus,
we are given a function and we have to find the derivative or differential of
this function, but in the integral calculus, we are to find a function whose
differential is given. Thus, integration is a process which is the inverse of
differentiation.

Let $\frac{d}{dx} F(x) = f(x)$ . Then we write $\int f(x) dx = F(x) + C$ . These integrals
are called indefinite integrals or general integrals, C is called constant of
integration. All these integrals differ by a constant.
$\diamond$ Some properties of indefinite integrals are as follows:

1. $\int [f(x) + g(x)] dx = \int f(x) dx + \int g(x) dx$

2. For any real number $k$, $\int k f(x) dx = k \int f(x) dx$

More generally, if $f_1, f_2, f_3, ... , f_n$ are functions and $k_1, k_2, ... , k_n$ are real
numbers. Then

$$\int [k_1 f_1(x) + k_2 f_2(x) + ... + k_n f_n(x)] dx$$

$$= k_1 \int f_1(x) dx + k_2 \int f_2(x) dx + ... + k_n \int f_n(x) dx$$

$\diamond$ Some standard integrals

(i) $\int x^n dx = \frac{x^{n+1}}{n+1} + C$, $n \neq -1$. Particularly, $\int dx = x + C$

blocks.label: List
blocks.text:
(ii) $\int \cos x \, dx = \sin x + \text{C}$                                     (iii) $\int \sin x \, dx = -\cos x + \text{C}$

(iv) $\int \sec^2 x \, dx = \tan x + \text{C}$                                     (v) $\int \text{cosec}^2 x \, dx = -\cot x + \text{C}$

(vi) $\int \sec x \tan x \, dx = \sec x + \text{C}$

(vii) $\int \text{cosec } x \cot x \, dx = -\text{cosec } x + \text{C}$      (viii) $\int \frac{dx}{\sqrt{1-x^2}} = \sin^{-1} x + \text{C}$

(ix) $\int \frac{dx}{\sqrt{1-x^2}} = -\cos^{-1} x + \text{C}$                                     (x) $\int \frac{dx}{1+x^2} = \tan^{-1} x + \text{C}$

(xi) $\int \frac{dx}{1+x^2} = -\cot^{-1} x + \text{C}$                                     (xii) $\int e^x \, dx = e^x + \text{C}$

(xiii) $\int a^x \, dx = \frac{a^x}{\log a} + \text{C}$                                     (xiv) $\int \frac{1}{x} \, dx = \log |x| + \text{C}$

blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: Integration by partial fractions

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Recall that a rational function is ratio of two polynomials of the form $\frac{\mathrm{P}(x)}{\mathrm{Q}(x)}$,
where $\mathrm{P}(x)$ and $\mathrm{Q}(x)$ are polynomials in $x$ and $\mathrm{Q}(x) \neq 0$. If degree of the
polynomial $\mathrm{P}(x)$ is greater than the degree of the polynomial $\mathrm{Q}(x)$, then we
may divide $\mathrm{P}(x)$ by $\mathrm{Q}(x)$ so that $\frac{\mathrm{P}(x)}{\mathrm{Q}(x)}=\mathrm{T}(x)+\frac{\mathrm{P}_{1}(x)}{\mathrm{Q}(x)}$, where $\mathrm{T}(x)$ is a
polynomial in $x$ and degree of $\mathrm{P}_{1}(x)$ is less than the degree of $\mathrm{Q}(x)$. $\mathrm{T}(x)$
being polynomial can be easily integrated. $\frac{\mathrm{P}_{1}(x)}{\mathrm{Q}(x)}$ can be integrated by

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: expressing $\frac{\mathrm{P}_{1}(x)}{\mathrm{Q}(x)}$ as the sum of partial fractions of the following type:

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$1. \quad \frac{px+q}{(x-a)(x-b)} \quad = \quad \frac{\mathrm{A}}{x-a} + \frac{\mathrm{B}}{x-b}, a \neq b$$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: 2. $\frac{px+q}{(x-a)^2} = \frac{A}{x-a} + \frac{B}{(x-a)^2}$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: 3. $\frac{px^2 + qx + r}{(x - a)(x - b)(x - c)} = \frac{\text{A}}{x - a} + \frac{\text{B}}{x - b} + \frac{\text{C}}{x - c}$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: 4. $\frac{px^2 + qx + r}{(x - a)^2 (x - b)} \quad = \quad \frac{\text{A}}{x - a} + \frac{\text{B}}{(x - a)^2} + \frac{\text{C}}{x - b}$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: 5. $\frac{px^2 + qx + r}{(x - a)(x^2 + bx + c)} = \frac{\text{A}}{x - a} + \frac{\text{Bx} + \text{C}}{x^2 + bx + c}$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: where $x^2 + bx + c$ can not be factorised further.

blocks.text: Integration by substitution

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
A change in the variable of integration often reduces an integral to one of the
fundamental integrals. The method in which we change the variable to some
other variable is called the method of substitution. When the integrand involves
some trigonometric functions, we use some well known identities to find the
integrals. Using substitution technique, we obtain the following standard
integrals.

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: (i) $\int \tan x \, dx = \log |\sec x| + \mathrm{C}$ \qquad (ii) $\int \cot x \, dx = \log |\sin x| + \mathrm{C}$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: (iii) $\int \sec x \, dx = \log |\sec x + \tan x| + \mathrm{C}$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: (iv) $\int \operatorname{cosec} x \, dx = \log |\operatorname{cosec} x - \cot x| + \mathrm{C}$

blocks.label: Sub-section-title
blocks.text: First fundamental theorem of integral calculus

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Let the area function be defined by $A(x) = \int_{a}^{x} f(x) dx$ for all $x \geq a$, where
the function $f$ is assumed to be continuous on $[a, b]$. Then $A'(x) = f(x)$ for all
$x \in [a, b]$.

blocks.label: List
blocks.text:
$\diamond$ **Second fundamental theorem of integral calculus**
Let $f$ be a continuous function of $x$ defined on the closed interval $[a, b]$ and

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: let F be another function such that $\frac{d}{dx} \mathrm{F}(x) = f(x)$ for all $x$ in the domain of

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$f, \text{ then } \int_{a}^{b} f(x) dx = [\mathrm{F}(x) + \mathrm{C}]_{a}^{b} = \mathrm{F}(b) - \mathrm{F}(a).$$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
This is called the definite integral of $f$ over the range $[a, b]$, where $a$ and $b$
are called the limits of integration, $a$ being the lower limit and $b$ the
upper limit.
